claims.claim: The long-term causes of World War I are commonly summarized as MAIN: militarism, alliances, imperialism, and nationalism; before 1914 Europe was divided into the Triple Entente (Russia, France, Britain) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy), with a naval arms race after Britain's 1906 HMS Dreadnought.

The immediate trigger of the war was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by a Bosnian Serb; Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, and alliance obligations then drew in Russia, Germany, France, and Britain within days.

After the Battle of the Marne (September 1914) the Western Front settled into trench warfare and stalemate; machine guns based on Hiram Maxim's 1884 design fired 400-600 rounds per minute, and poison gases (chlorine, mustard, phosgene), heavy artillery, tanks (introduced by Britain in 1916), and aircraft made the fighting deadly.

World War I was a total war, defined by OpenStax as a war fought using all available resources with no restrictions on weapons or their targets, mobilizing whole economies and civilian populations; it was global in scope, with empires drawing troops and resources from colonies across Africa, Asia, and the Pacific.
The human cost was staggering: estimates attributed to the Imperial War Museum put military deaths above nine million, wounded around twenty-one million, and civilian deaths close to ten million.
The 1918 influenza pandemic spread among troops and worldwide; the U.S. CDC estimates it killed at least 50 million people globally.

Fighting ended with an armistice that took effect on 11 November 1918; the Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, imposed war guilt on Germany via Article 231 plus reparations, territorial losses, and disarmament, and its harshness is widely seen as contributing to conditions leading to World War II.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The relative weight of the causes of World War I and how much blame the Treaty of Versailles bears for World War II
positions: Historians agree on the sequence and dates of 1914 but continue to debate which underlying causes mattered most and how much German responsibility Article 231 fairly assigned.

Most historians see the treaty's harsh terms as feeding German resentment that helped enable World War II, but they disagree on how decisive the treaty was versus later economic and political factors.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the dates and sequence as established fact and presents the weighting of causes and the Versailles-to-WWII link as widely held interpretation that historians still debate, without declaring one view correct.

positions: Military death estimates commonly range around 9-10 million; civilian deaths are estimated in the millions up to about 10 million; 1918 flu deaths are estimated at 50 million or more.
Figures vary by source and methodology and cannot be stated as exact counts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All casualty figures are given as attributed estimates and ranges, not precise counts.
